questions.q: Electric current is the rate of flow of:
questions.solution:
$I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$ — current is **charge per second**, measured in amperes.

One ampere is one coulomb per second.

$\mathbf{V = IR}$ — and the resistance is constant only if the temperature is.

A filament lamp does **not** obey Ohm's law: as it heats up its resistance rises, so its $V$–$I$ graph curves.

questions.q: In a series circuit, the current:
questions.solution:
One path, so the **same current** flows through every component.

It is the **voltage** that divides, in proportion to each component's resistance. Charge cannot pile up anywhere, so what goes in must come out.

questions.q: The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by:
questions.solution:
A **soft iron core** magnetises strongly and greatly increases the field.

More turns and more current also help. Iron is chosen over steel because it **loses** its magnetism the moment the current stops — which is what lets a scrapyard crane drop what it picked up.

questions.q: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force. Its direction is given by:
questions.solution:
**Fleming's left-hand rule**, for the motor effect.

**F**irst finger = **F**ield, se**C**ond finger = **C**urrent, thu**M**b = **M**otion.

The right-hand rule is for the **generator**, where motion produces current.

questions.q: A resistor of $8\,\Omega$ carries a current of $1.5$ A. Find the voltage across it, in volts.
Resistors of $4\,\Omega$ and $6\,\Omega$ are connected in series. Find the total resistance, in ohms.
Resistors of $4\,\Omega$ and $12\,\Omega$ are connected in parallel. Find the total resistance, in ohms.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac14 + \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{3 + 1}{12} = \dfrac13$, so $R = \mathbf{3}\,\Omega$.

Less than the smaller of the two, as a parallel combination always is.

questions.q: Find the power (in watts) of a device drawing $3$ A from a $12$ V supply.
A current of $2$ A flows for $30$ s. Find the charge that passes, in coulombs.
Compare series and parallel circuits in terms of current, voltage and resistance, and explain why houses are wired in parallel.
questions.solution:
**Series circuit**

• **Current:** the same through every component.

• **Voltage:** divides between them, in proportion to resistance.

• **Resistance:** $R = R_{1} + R_{2}$ — always **more** than the largest.

• One break stops **everything**.

**Parallel circuit**

• **Current:** divides between the branches; the smallest resistance takes the most.

• **Voltage:** the **same** across every branch.

• **Resistance:** $\dfrac1R = \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}$ — always **less** than the smallest.

• One break affects **only that branch**.

**Why houses are wired in parallel — three reasons:**

1. **Every appliance receives the full mains voltage.** In series they would share it, and each device would run weakly.

2. **Each can be switched independently.** In series, switching one off would break the circuit and everything would go out.

3. **Each draws the current it needs**, from a kettle's $10$ A to a lamp's fraction of an amp, without being limited by the others.

The cost is that adding appliances lowers the total resistance and raises the total current, which is why a circuit can be **overloaded** and why fuses exist.

questions.q: Describe the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire and inside a solenoid, and explain how an electromagnet is used in a relay.
questions.solution:
**Around a straight wire.** The field lines are **concentric circles** in a plane perpendicular to the wire, stronger nearer the wire.

Direction from the **right-hand grip rule**: thumb along the current, fingers curl the way the field goes.

**Inside a solenoid.** A coil of many turns produces a **strong, uniform** field inside with parallel field lines, and a weak field outside — exactly like a **bar magnet**, with a north and a south end.

Strengthened by: more turns, more current, and a **soft iron core**.

**A relay** uses a small current to switch a large one.

1. A small current flows through the electromagnet's coil.

2. The electromagnet attracts a pivoted **iron armature**.

3. The armature closes the contacts of a **separate** circuit, switching on a much larger current.

4. When the small current stops, the soft iron **loses its magnetism at once** and a spring pulls the contacts open again.

**Why this matters.** The two circuits are **electrically isolated**, so a safe low voltage at a switch can control a dangerous high-current circuit — a car's starter motor, or an industrial machine.

Soft iron is essential here: steel would stay magnetised and the relay would never switch off.

questions.topic: The motor effect and the generator
questions.q: Explain the motor effect and the working of a d.c. motor, then explain electromagnetic induction and how a generator differs.
questions.solution:
**The motor effect.** A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a **force**, because the field of the current interacts with the field of the magnet.

Direction by **Fleming's left-hand rule**; the force is greatest when the wire is at right angles to the field, and zero when it lies along it.

**The d.c. motor.**

1. A coil in a magnetic field carries a current.

2. The two sides carry current in opposite directions, so one is pushed **up** and the other **down** — the coil turns.

3. After a half turn the sides have swapped, and the forces would now oppose the rotation.

4. The **split-ring commutator** reverses the current at exactly that moment, so the push stays in step and the rotation continues.

**Electromagnetic induction — the reverse process.** Moving a magnet near a coil, or a wire through a field, **induces a voltage**.

The induced voltage is larger for a faster movement, a stronger magnet or more turns — and it is zero when nothing is moving.

**Lenz's law:** the induced current always **opposes** the change producing it. That is conservation of energy: the work done pushing against that opposition is exactly the electrical energy generated. If it helped instead, you would get energy from nothing.

**Generator against motor.** Mechanically they are the same machine, run in opposite directions: a motor takes electrical energy and gives motion, a generator takes motion and gives electrical energy.

An a.c. generator uses **slip rings** so the output alternates; a d.c. one uses a **commutator** to keep it one way.

questions.q: Describe the three wires in a mains cable, explain the purpose of the earth wire and the fuse, and say why double-insulated appliances need no earth.
questions.solution:
**The three wires.**

• **Live (brown)** — carries the alternating supply at $230$ V. The dangerous one.

• **Neutral (blue)** — completes the circuit, at about $0$ V.

• **Earth (green and yellow)** — a safety wire connected to the metal case and to the ground. Normally carries **no current at all**.

**The earth wire.** If a fault lets the live wire touch the metal case, the case becomes live and anyone touching it would receive a shock.

The earth wire gives that current a path of **very low resistance** straight to the ground, so a huge current flows — which blows the fuse and disconnects the appliance.

The earth wire does not merely protect; it **reveals** the fault.

**The fuse.** A thin wire that melts when the current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit before the cable overheats. It must be fitted in the **live** wire — in the neutral, the appliance would remain connected to $230$ V after it blew.

Choose the next standard rating **above** the normal working current: a $3$ A fuse for a lamp, $13$ A for a kettle.

**Double insulation.** The appliance has a plastic case, or its metal parts are enclosed in an insulating layer, so **no exposed part can ever become live**.

There is nothing to earth, so these appliances have a two-core cable and are marked with a **double square** symbol. A hairdryer or an electric drill is usually of this kind.

questions.q: Explain how a transformer works, write the turns equation, and explain why electricity is transmitted at high voltage.
questions.solution:
**How it works.** Two coils are wound on a common soft-iron core.

1. Alternating current in the **primary** coil creates a **changing** magnetic field in the core.

2. The core carries that changing field to the **secondary** coil.

3. The changing field **induces** an alternating voltage in the secondary.

**A transformer works on a.c. only.** With d.c. the field would be steady, nothing would change, and nothing would be induced.

**Turns equation:**

$\dfrac{V_{s}}{V_{p}} = \dfrac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$

More turns on the secondary **steps up** the voltage; fewer **steps down**.

**Power is conserved** in an ideal transformer: $V_{p}I_{p} = V_{s}I_{s}$. So stepping the voltage **up** steps the current **down** in the same proportion — a transformer gives nothing away.

**Why transmit at high voltage.** Power lost as heat in the cables is $P = I^{2}R$ — proportional to the **square** of the current.

Step the voltage up by a factor of 100 and the current falls by 100, so the loss falls by a factor of **10 000**.

That is why the National Grid runs at $400$ kV, and why step-down transformers are needed at every substation to bring it back to a voltage safe enough to enter a house.
